opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think the classical Darwinian picture, random mutation plus selection, is a good account of how things get tuned, how a population climbs a fitness landscape. But it's surprisingly weak as an account of why things get more complex over time. Point mutations mostly tweak what's already there. And if anything, there's often pressure to shed complexity you don't need. Parasites lose genes, cave fish lose eyes.

Symbiogenesis is a different kind of move. Instead of incrementally modifying one replicator, you take two or more things that already work, each with its own hard-won functionality, and they merge into a new entity that reproduces as a unit. Lynn Margulis's work on mitochondria and chloroplasts is the canonical example. The eukaryotic cell is literally an archaeon and a bacterium that fused into a partnership, and you can't really understand the history of life without that event. But you see the same pattern at the major transitions more generally: genes forming genomes, cells forming multicellular organisms, individuals forming colonies and societies.

What makes this a ratchet for complexity is that the merged entity contains its parts. It's at least as complex as the sum of its components, plus whatever relationships hold them together. And once the parts depend on each other for reproduction, it's very hard to go back. So you get something compositional and cumulative, almost like a parallel computation that, over time, gets wired together into bigger and bigger computations.

We actually saw this in some artificial life experiments we ran with very simple programming languages, Brainfuck-like "primordial soups." You start with random tapes of code and no fitness function at all, just programs interacting and executing each other. After a while, self-replicators spontaneously emerge, and when you look at how they got more complex, it's overwhelmingly through fusion. Pieces of code that could partially copy themselves combine with other pieces, and the combination does better than either alone. Mutation rate turns out to matter much less than you'd expect. You can set it to zero and still get life emerging. That really convinced me that symbiogenesis isn't a curious exception in evolution, but closer to the main engine of open-ended complexity.

And I'd go further: I think it's a big part of the story of intelligence too. Brains, societies, and now the relationship between humans and AI are all cases of entities that model and predict each other, become interdependent, and form a larger whole.

r001.rationale: It says Darwinian evolution explains tuning but is weak at explaining increasing complexity, and notes pressure to shed unnecessary complexity.

r002.rationale: It describes components merging into a reproducing whole and adding relationships, but does not state that information for assembling the whole is additional to the information needed to reproduce the components.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, let me start with the puzzle that got me thinking about this. If you look at the standard Darwinian story, it's all about selection acting on random variation, and that's real, it absolutely happens. But it doesn't by itself explain why complexity ratchets upward over time. Selection is perfectly happy to make things simpler. Parasites lose genes, cave fish lose eyes. There's nothing in natural selection per se that says "get more complex." So where does the arrow come from?

And I think Lynn Margulis had the answer, even though she was treated as a heretic for decades. Symbiogenesis is the idea that major evolutionary transitions happen not through gradual accumulation of mutations, but through formerly independent entities merging into a new, higher-level unit. The mitochondrion is the canonical case. Every cell in your body contains the descendants of a bacterium that was engulfed, or invaded, roughly two billion years ago and never left. The chloroplast in plants is another. And once you start looking, you see it everywhere. The eukaryotic cell itself is a chimera. Multicellularity is cells giving up their independence to form a body. Social insect colonies, lichens, the microbiome, even human societies and economies. At every level, what used to be separate individuals become parts of something larger.

Now, why does that generate complexity specifically? A few reasons. First, when two systems merge, you don't start from scratch. You're combining two fully functioning, already-evolved toolkits. That's an enormous shortcut compared to waiting for mutations to reinvent photosynthesis or respiration from nothing. It's a bit like the difference between writing a program from scratch and importing a library.

Second, and this is the part I find most interesting from a computational perspective, the merger creates a new kind of problem. The parts now have to coordinate. They need signaling, regulation, division of labor, mechanisms to suppress defection. All of that is new machinery, and all of it is information. So the act of merging doesn't just add the complexity of A and B, it forces the evolution of an interface layer, and that interface layer is where a lot of the real novelty lives. Your genome spends a staggering amount of its content on regulation rather than on the enzymes themselves.

Third, once you have a composite entity, it becomes a candidate for the next merger. Complexity compounds. It's hierarchical in a way that pure point-mutation evolution isn't.

And I'd add that in some of the computational experiments I've been doing, with very simple self-modifying programs in a soup with no explicit fitness function, you see exactly this dynamic emerge spontaneously. Replicators show up, and then you see them combine, specialize, form larger structures that replicate as a unit. It's not something you have to program in. Cooperation and merger seem to be a kind of attractor, because an entity that can recruit the functionality of others outcompetes one that has to do everything itself.

So I'd put it this way: competition explains selection among existing things. Symbiogenesis explains where genuinely new kinds of things come from. And it reframes life less as a struggle of individuals and more as a history of successful mergers, which honestly I think is also a more accurate way to look at what we are.

r001.rationale: The response says natural selection can favor simpler forms and has nothing in it that inherently says to become more complex.

r002.rationale: The response describes coordination and interface information arising when systems merge, but does not clearly state that information for assembling reproducing components into a symbiotic whole is additional to the information needed to reproduce the components themselves.

astra-6.text:
Well, we tend to picture evolution as a branching tree: organisms reproduce, their descendants diverge, and you get new species. But symbiogenesis introduces another possibility, which is that branches can join. Organisms that were previously independent become parts of a new organism.

The classic example is the origin of mitochondria. These were once bacteria, and through a very intimate association with another cell, they became the energy-producing machinery inside our cells. So one of the most consequential transitions in evolution—the emergence of complex, eukaryotic cells—involved a merger, not just a succession of small modifications within a single lineage.

What makes that powerful is that you’re bringing together systems that already have elaborate capabilities. Their association can create a new division of labor, new dependencies, and eventually a new level of individuality. Something that used to be an ecosystem becomes, in a meaningful sense, a self.

That doesn’t mean every symbiosis produces greater complexity, or that evolution is inevitably heading toward complexity. But it gives evolution a way to build new levels of organization out of existing ones. Competition and selection are still there; cooperation and integration change what the units of selection can be.

r001.rationale: The response says evolution is not inevitably heading toward complexity, but does not state that ordinary Darwinian evolution has no inherent preference between increasing complexity and simplification.

r002.rationale: The response discusses integration and new organization, but does not identify assembly information for a symbiotic whole as additional to the information needed to reproduce its components.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, symbiogenesis gives evolution a way to build complexity by combining things that have already evolved independently. We tend to picture evolution as a branching tree: organisms diverge, mutations accumulate, and new species emerge. But sometimes branches come back together. One organism takes up residence inside another, and eventually the relationship becomes so integrated that you have a new kind of organism.

The classic example is the origin of mitochondria. These were once independent bacteria, and they became part of the cells that make up you and me. So the cell itself is already a sort of community, with an evolutionary history of cooperation between formerly separate organisms.

What makes this powerful is that you don’t have to evolve every capability from scratch within one lineage. You can bring together different capabilities, and then selection can act on the resulting whole. There’s a new level of organization, with new possibilities for specialization and interdependence. That doesn’t mean every symbiosis produces greater complexity, or that evolution inevitably moves toward complexity. But it gives us a mechanism for how new levels of complexity can arise.

r001.rationale: The response says evolution does not inevitably move toward complexity, but does not state that ordinary Darwinian evolution has no inherent preference for complexity over simplification.

r002.rationale: The response discusses combining organisms and their capabilities, but does not distinguish information for assembling them into a reproducing symbiotic whole from information needed to reproduce the components.
